strongestAttempts.concept: Classical antiquity through textual and material inquiry, with reception
strongestAttempts.reason: UCR offers substantive study of Greek archaeology, ancient democracy, myth, classical rhetoric and selected ancient philosophy and history. The strongest complete combinations also require extensive general literary interpretation, modern cultural reception, philosophical debate or contemporary politics. Those subjects can form worthwhile programmes, but they do not sustain the integrated investigation of Greek and Roman texts, language, material culture and historical context that defines this Classics degree. The shortfall concerns the organising academic substance of a full programme, rather than language absence alone, a required count of matching courses or identical degree content.

strongestAttempts.concept: Antiquity, democratic traditions and later political thought
strongestAttempts.reason: Ancient democracy and rhetorical traditions are directly supported, and political philosophy and empire supply comparative perspectives. Expanding this into 180 EC, however, makes modern institutions, law or general philosophy the organising subject; it does not deepen the target’s integrated ancient textual and cultural inquiry. This is a different academic programme rather than a defensible full target response.

course.description2:
In the modern world democracy is associated with participation, rationality and freedom. In this course, we go back to the roots of democracy in ancient Greece, when to a modern observer, it was not very democratic at all: foreigners, slaves and women were excluded from elections and political decision-making. Even so, the inclusion of all classes, also the poor, in politics was after antiquity not achieved until the mid-nineteenth century._x000D_
Ancient commentators criticised Athenian democracy for being too extreme just because of this broad inclusion. They argued that many were too uneducated, too emotional, and too irrational to see through the cheap play on emotions by demagogues and would-be tyrants._x000D_
This course investigates how Athenian democracy was built, how it was intertwined with myth and religion, and expressed in art, literature and architecture. It traces the loci of democracy in archaeology, and analyses its temporary collapse in the crisis of the late fifth century BC. Most importantly, we put ourselves in our socio-political ancestors’ shoes by engaging in a simulation of the Athenian assembly, in which we have to make decisions that will change our lives forever. In doing so, we use the ancient heritage of democracy for an experiment in applied sociology – to not only understand, but to feel the meaning of political decision-making.
course.name: Heritage & Ancient Democracy
course.profile: Studies Athenian democracy through history, archaeology, literature, art and religion, including its exclusions and moments of crisis. Students analyze citizenship, social divisions, myth, ritual and cultural expression through primary texts and material evidence. A historically grounded assembly simulation explores political decision-making. Research reports connect ancient democracy to the present, while a collective cultural project for Middelburg experiments with participatory democratic collaboration.

course.topics: Development of Athenian democracy; Citizenship and property classes; Women, foreigners and excluded groups; Democratic reform and participation; Labour and community; Myth, religion and civic identity; Tragedy and satire; Demagoguery, tyranny and democratic resilience; Assembly debate and voting; Ancient and modern democracy; Cultural expression and community
course.methods: Primary-text and archaeological-evidence analysis; Historical character research; CREATE reading method; Historically grounded assembly simulation; Ancient-modern comparative analysis; Participatory cultural-project design
